cap: Read the graph from top to bottom. GnRH pulses run fast before ovulation and slow after it, because progesterone slows them. FSH peaks early to recruit follicles, estradiol from the dominant follicle peaks about a day before the LH surge, and progesterone from the corpus luteum peaks about 7 days after ovulation, on day 21. The endometrium follows the steroids: proliferative under estradiol, secretory under progesterone, shed when both fall. Basal body temperature steps up after ovulation.
teach: How to identify each hormone: LH is the sharp spike near day 14, and ovulation follows about 10 to 12 hours after its peak. FSH is high at the start of the cycle, has a small mid-cycle rise and falls in the luteal phase. Estradiol has two humps: a tall one just before the LH surge, from the dominant follicle, and a smaller second rise in the mid-luteal phase, from the corpus luteum. Progesterone stays near zero until ovulation and peaks about day 21. GnRH is released in pulses, so the clue is pulse frequency: fast pulses before ovulation favor LH, and slow pulses in the luteal phase, restrained by progesterone, favor the FSH rise that starts the next cycle.
